newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS-KLM CEO to quit as year net slides.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-KLM CEO to quit as year net slides.

text.p: KLM Royal Dutch Airlines said on Wednesday its profits fell sharply in 1996-97 as runaway costs outpaced revenue growth and its bottom line was hit by a hefty restructuring charge aimed at boosting future earnings.
KLM also unexpectedly said its president and chief executive Pieter Bouw would stand down in August after six years at the helm to allow a colleague to oversee a crucial recovery plan.
Net profit for the year to March 31 fell to 236 million guilders ($125.2 million) from 547 million.
This included a pre-tax provision of 290 million for the Focus 2000 restructuring programme which aims to boost operating income by 1.5 billion guilders over the next three years.
But Bouw told a results news conference this was not the only factor behind the drop in earnings.
"Operating results, which reflect what we earn from our network...have declined to an extremely meagre amount of 89 million guilders from 453 million," he said.

Operating costs rose 13.1 percent over the year, significantly outpacing an 8.6 percent rise in operating revenues, he noted. KLM figures showed fuel costs spiralled 29 percent higher during the year, and wages rose 11 percent.
But Bouw said the Focus 2000 programme was progressing according to schedule with 45 out of 74 projects up and running and would start yielding results during the current 1997-98 year.
"Important advantages may be expected during the current year and even more in the year thereafter," he said.
KLM said Bouw, 55, would resign as CEO at the annual meeting on August 5 and that its supervisory board planned to appoint chief operating officer Leo van Wijk, 50, to succeed him.
Answering a question, Bouw said his resignation was in no way linked to KLM's poor operating performance in recent years.
"Results have lagged expectations, but if you look at operating results of other (airline) companies...you will see they are in a similar position," he said.

He said his decision to step down had been motivated by a belief that top posts in a fast-changing industry should not be held too long by the same person and the fact that the Focus 2000 programme was well on track.
"The target is known and we are on our way," he said.

He said Focus 2000 was not merely a cost cutting operation but a total reorientation of the group's priorities, with two thirds of the envisaged operating profits lift coming from extra revenues and only one third from cost cutting.
The slide in KLM's 1996-97 earnings came despite a higher contribution from its U.S. associate Northwest Airlines (NWA) of 442 million guilders versus 258 million in 1995-96.

This was mainly derived from the sale and revaluation of various types of NWA shares, but the fourth quarter also brought 59 million guilders in operational profits from Northwest following NWA's return to positive equity.
KLM said it expected 1997-98 operating income to show a significant improvement.
"On balance we expect for 1997-98 a significant improvement in operating income from the present unsatisfactory base," it said in a statement.
It said its forecast was based on the assumption of a positive economic climate and a lower fuel price following a 29 percent increase in fuel costs in 1995-96.
Analysts were unimpressed by KLM's results. While the bottom-line figure came in close to their forecasts, most analysts had not reckoned on a contribution from KLM's 18.8 percent Northwest stake.
"At first, I thought these results were more or less in line (with expectations)," said Richard Brakenhoff of MeesPierson.

"However, if you look at the breakdown, operating profit was quite disappointing. That's offset by the contribution from Northwest Airlines . Some of the cost items were higher than expected," he said.
Nevertheless, KLM shares rose on a strongly higher Amsterdam bourse, coasting up 1.30 guilders at 59.50 by 1250 GMT off an earlier high of 60.70.
Dealers attributed this to the news that Leo van Wijk, regarded as a wily strategist, was set to take over from Bouw.
